title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Morality in the Thames

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, ambitious look at one of the greatest and strangest novels in the English language.
Our Mutual Friend was Charles Dickens's last completed novel, published in the mid-1860s — and it is, by almost any measure, his most radical.
Money, death, identity, the Thames — this novel takes all of it and makes something genuinely unsettling and alive.
Joining me today are three people whose company I could not be more grateful for.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a watch — for the extraordinary precision of how it's built.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees every institution in a novel as a mechanism of class power — and who thinks Dickens was more radical than even Dickens suspected.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than any reasonable person should attempt — approaches every page as a performer who wants to know what the prose sounds like in the air.
Our theme today is money and morality — the axis around which the whole novel turns.
Daniel, I want to start with you, because the novel opens in a world of spectacular, almost theatrical fakery — and you've been looking at a passage that captures that perfectly.
Thank you — yes, and I think this is the essential entry point into the novel's moral universe.

Dickens gives us the Veneerings — this family conjured from nowhere, whose entire social existence is pure performance — and then he gives us Lady Tippins, who is the performance's most self-aware cheerleader.
She clatters around town drumming up votes for Veneering's parliamentary campaign, and she does it while openly, gleefully, confessing the entire thing is a charade.
Listen to the extraordinary candour of what she says.

"And we are carrying on this little farce to keep up appearances, and isn't it refreshing! Then, my precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights."
Nobody knows who these Veneerings are — she says it herself, in the middle of campaigning for them.
This is Dickens's portrait of a ruling class that has abandoned even the pretence of legitimacy — and what's terrifying is that the system works anyway.
It's almost vertiginous, isn't it — a satire so sharp it almost becomes a confession.
Eleanor, does that passage strike you as something Dickens constructed with particular care?
Enormously — it's a masterclass in what I'd call delegated satire.
Dickens doesn't need to tell us the Veneerings are frauds — he hands that job to Lady Tippins, who performs the exposure while performing the campaign.
And the sentence architecture is doing something marvellous — it mimics her voice perfectly, all that breathless accumulation.
"My exclusive property, the dearest friends I have in the world" — the possessives pile up until they become openly absurd.
She's commodifying friendship in real time, and the rhythm of the prose enacts exactly that.
I have to say, having read Lady Tippins aloud more times than is strictly healthy, that passage is a genuine gift to a performer.
The rhythm accelerates and then that little landing — "I call their dinner-table, the Caravan" — it's pure comic timing built into the punctuation.
But what makes it extraordinary is that Dickens keeps the joke alive while Daniel's critique is simultaneously true.
The comedy and the horror are inseparable — and that is very much the novel's register throughout.
Oliver puts his finger on something I want to hold for a moment — because the novel isn't only comic.
Running alongside this glittering social satire is another story entirely — a story about a man pulled under the Thames and fighting his way back to the surface.
John Harmon's recovery of consciousness is one of the most viscerally written passages in the novel.
Dickens writes it as a kind of interior command — the self ordering itself to survive.
"This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon, struggle for your life. John Harmon, call on Heaven and save yourself!"
Three times the name — like a desperate act of self-reconstitution.
And this matters enormously because the entire plot turns on whether John Harmon can remain himself — or whether the world's demand that he perform an identity will swallow him whole.
That repetition of the name is structurally crucial — it creates the character's very selfhood in extremis.
There's something almost liturgical about it — invoking one's own name as a kind of prayer.
And notice that consciousness arrives as reported speech — "the consciousness came upon me" — which gives the character a vertiginous distance from his own survival instinct.
Dickens is engineering the sensation of near-death from the inside — and it's a genuinely modern technique.
Reading that passage aloud is something you never forget — the three iterations of the name demand a different weight each time.
First — recognition. Second — command. Third — something almost like a cry to God.
And then Dickens cuts to: "it was I who was struggling there alone in the water" — that lonely pronoun, after all that desperate naming, is devastating.
There's a third passage Daniel has been sitting with — one that pulls these threads together in a way that's almost painterly.
Daniel — tell us what Dickens is doing with light and colour just before the violence comes.
This is Bradley Headstone pursuing Eugene Wrayburn along the river — a scene that exists on the knife-edge between the symbolic and the brutally physical.
Dickens turns the landscape itself into a moral statement — the sun sets and floods everything red.
And then comes a line of absolute, cold authority.
"And then the red had the appearance of fading out of it and mounting up to Heaven, as we say that blood, guiltily shed, does."
"As we say" — Dickens makes us complicit, invoking a collective moral language that everyone knows and almost nobody lives by.
The violence isn't just coming — it's already written into the sky, into the water, into the very grammar of the sentence.
That phrase "guiltily shed" does something architecturally precise — it assigns guilt in a subordinate clause, almost as an aside, before the crime has even happened.
The syntax performs the moral verdict in advance.
That is extraordinary craft — the sentence is the judgement.
And it slows everything down — that long vowel sequence, "fading... mounting... Heaven" — it's almost unbearable to read at pace.
The reader is being made to feel the weight of what's coming before they can name it.
Money performed for an audience, identity clawed back from drowning, violence foretold in the colour of the sky — and we're still in the opening.
In our next segment, we go deeper into the social machinery — the nouveaux riches, the dinner table as theatre, and what all that gold and silver actually costs.

segments.title: Bella's Price: The Architecture of a Woman's Fall and Rise

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as the strange, brilliant, troubling masterpiece it is.
Today we're deep inside what I think is the novel's most psychologically intricate thread: the education of Bella Wilfer.
A young woman bequeathed to a stranger by a dead man's will — and the long, uncomfortable journey from mercenary fantasy to something far harder to name.
To unpack this, I'm joined by three exceptional readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar who cares deeply about how sentences are built — and why that architecture matters.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian for whom every novel is also a map of class power — who gains, who loses, and at whose expense.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone should reasonably attempt — brings the novelist's rhythms to life as performance.
Let's begin at the source: a man lying in a public-house bed, constructing a fiction that will remake a woman's life without her knowledge.
What strikes me first about the John Harmon soliloquy is how Dickens frames an act of profound paternalism as though it were entirely reasonable.
Harmon recounts his calculation — and notice that word, 'calculation' — with the careful logic of a man who has already decided.
The sentence that reveals everything is this one — listen to its structure:
'the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella.' Two words at the end of a very long sentence — and they carry the whole moral weight of the novel's central plot.
She is to be tested. She doesn't know she's being tested. And the tester has appointed himself with no authority other than inheritance and desire.
Dickens gives us the logic in Harmon's own voice — and it's seductive logic — but the architecture of that sentence quietly indicts it.
Eleanor is absolutely right about the indictment — and I'd push it further.
What Harmon calls 'moral timidity' is in fact the ideology of property speaking through him.
The 'fate' he fears — that his father's riches 'should lead to nothing but evil' — is displaced entirely onto Bella's character.
The system that produced those riches, the labour that created them, the river that yields and destroys — none of that is examined.
A woman must be refined and tested so that the money may be enjoyed with a clear conscience. That is the transaction.
And Dickens — to his immense credit — makes the machinery visible, even when his plot ultimately rewards Harmon for running it.
I want to come in on the performance of that passage, because there's something Dickens does rhythmically that I find quite devilish.
Harmon speaks in these long, winding, self-justifying periods — the syntax of a man rehearsing his own innocence.
When you read it aloud, you feel the effort of it — every subordinate clause a small evasion.
And yet the novel also gives us a scene that cuts right through that elaborate self-justification with pure comic ferocity.
Mr Boffin on the subject of charity patronage — I defy anyone to read this without audible pleasure:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The accumulation of titles — Deceased Patrons! Ex-Vice-Patronesses! — is a comic avalanche, and it buries the entire institution of charitable giving under its own pomposity.
That passage is a masterclass in satirical listing — Dickens understood that repetition, pushed far enough, becomes ridicule.
But what I find remarkable is the dramatic function of Boffin's speech in Bella's arc.
He's performing — or beginning to perform — a worldview: money as the only honest god.
And the novel crystallises that worldview in a speech so blunt it almost sounds like parody of itself:
'Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.'
The rhythm of 'R—r—rich!' at the end — that stuttering relish — is the novel's most disturbing sound effect.
It's grotesque, and it's meant to be. The question is what Bella hears when she listens to it.
And this is where Dickens does something genuinely radical, I think.
Because Bella's response to Boffin's sermon on money is not simple revulsion. It is far more uncomfortable than that.
She goes to her room, sits before her mirror, and stages a cross-examination of herself that the novel renders in free indirect speech of brilliant precision:

'Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?'
'You inconsistent little Beast.' She recognises the value system as her own — and is appalled by the recognition.
That is ideology becoming conscious of itself. And ideology that can see itself begins — only begins — to crack.
The mirror scene is one of my absolute favourites in the novel, because Dickens gives Bella two voices simultaneously — judge and defendant.
And when you perform it, you have to find that split — the Bella who says 'very sensible, very true,' and the Bella who recoils from what she's just said.
The comedy is real — 'you inconsistent little Beast' is a magnificent insult to deliver to yourself — but the discomfort underneath it is also real.
And Dickens doesn't let her off the hook. The novel then arranges an encounter that strikes far closer to home — Bella with Lizzie Hexam.
That encounter between Bella and Lizzie is, to my mind, the hinge of Bella's entire transformation — and I want to hear from all three of you on it.
There's a moment of almost physical moral reckoning — Bella literally pokes herself in repentance.
The penitential poke! It is one of the funniest and most precisely observed moments in the book.
Here is the exact moment — and the narration earns every word of it:
'There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?'
What's extraordinary is that this is directed inward — Bella scolding Bella — while she physically punishes herself with 'a penitential poke in the side.'
Dickens embodies moral consciousness. The body responds before the intellect can catch up with what the heart already knows.
And the comedy — the poke! — is what makes it bearable, what allows Bella, and us, to inhabit the shame without being crushed by it.
And what Lizzie says to provoke that poke is itself extraordinary — because it's about Eugene Wrayburn, and it is the most quietly devastating declaration of love in the novel.
Lizzie describes a love she knows is hopeless, knows is dangerous, and yet refuses to disown.
She says — and this wants reading slowly:
'I would not have the light of them taken out of my life, for anything my life can give me.'
'The light of them.' Not the memory of him. Not love, not hope. The light — something ambient, permanent, irreplaceable.
It's one of those lines that reminds you Dickens could, when he chose, write with the compression of a lyric poet.
I want to put Lizzie and Bella in the same frame for a moment, because the contrast is structural, not merely sentimental.
Lizzie Hexam is a woman with nothing — no money, no class position, no protection — who holds to a love she knows may destroy her.
Bella Wilfer is a woman who has been offered everything, and is in the process of discovering that 'everything' denominated in money is a very impoverished everything indeed.
Dickens places these two women in a room together not to moralize directly but to let the contrast do its work on Bella — and on us.
The 'penitential poke' is funny, yes — but it is also the first genuinely free act Bella performs in the novel.
That phrase — 'the first genuinely free act' — feels like exactly the right place to mark the turn in Bella's story.
She begins, in that room with Lizzie, to want something other than what she was told to want.
In our next segment, we'll trace what Dickens builds on that foundation — and ask whether the architecture fully supports the moral vision it promises.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps Speak: Boffin's Encounter with Greed

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we dig into Dickens's last completed novel — a book as dense and glittering as the dust heaps at its centre.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers of this novel, each bringing a completely different lens to the text.
Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing scholar whose great gift is showing us how the machinery of a great novel actually works — the architecture beneath the surface.
Daniel Rosen reads novels as anatomies of class and power — and Our Mutual Friend, with its mountains of refuse and its rivers of money, is almost tailor-made for his particular fury.

And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, narrator of more classic audiobooks than any person should reasonably have time for — hears this novel the way Dickens almost certainly heard it himself: as performance, as rhythm, as voice.
Today's segment concerns Nicodemus Boffin — the Golden Dustman — and the extraordinary satirical machinery Dickens deploys around his sudden wealth.
The dust heaps have made him rich, and now everyone wants a piece — from dukes to despairing widows to a man who will be cold in death at a quarter to one on Tuesday.
Eleanor, let's begin with the basic situation — Boffin installed in his mansion — because Dickens gives us an image almost immediately that tells us everything about this world.
He really does — and it's one of those Dickens images that seems throwaway until you realise it's doing the work of an entire essay.
Dickens introduces Boffin in the mansion with this devastating parenthetical about his feelings toward the place.
"Like an eminently aristocratic family cheese, it was much too large for his wants, and bred an infinite amount of parasites."
The cheese — this is the joke that earns its keep at every level simultaneously.
The aristocratic family is the cheese — aged, overblown, its very grandeur a kind of rot.
And the parasites it breeds — that's everyone who is about to descend on Boffin from the very next page onward.
Dickens plants the entire thematic engine of the next hundred pages inside a comic simile about dairy produce.
That is craft of an almost reckless confidence.
And notice the narrator's voice in that passage — "the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour" — before catching himself and saying "or in less cutting language, Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire."
That "or in less cutting language" is pure music — a comedian stepping out from behind the curtain for half a beat and then stepping back.
When you're reading this aloud — and I have, many times — you have to resist the urge to milk it.
The joke is already perfectly timed; your job is simply to get out of its way.
And then the next sequence — the letters, the appeals, the charities — that's where Dickens really opens the throttle.
The Duke of Linseed's letter is a set piece of the first order.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Seven words — no verb — and you can see the whole thing sitting on the Secretary's desk, self-important and absurd.
What strikes me most fiercely about that sequence is the economics beneath the comedy.
Look at the catalogue before we even get to the Duke — fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, twenty-seven organs, twelve hundred children.
Each of these institutions is extracting money upward — from Boffin, yes, but originally from the poor whose labour made the dust heaps valuable in the first place.
And the Duke's three-guinea fee is the purest example: charity laundering aristocratic prestige on the backs of working wealth.
Dickens tells us the letter was "lithographed by the hundred" — a form letter — and yet it speaks of Boffin as "popular and distinguished."
The condescension is structural: the Duke cannot even be bothered to personalise his extraction.
This is Dickens showing us that charity, as practised by the English ruling class, is simply a mechanism of class reproduction dressed in the language of virtue.
And then Dickens pivots from the institutional beggars to the individual ones — and the prose actually changes gear.
There's this wonderful moment where Dickens — through the Secretary — anatomises the letters people send with their so-called supporting documents.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf — again, the food image, the reduction to something meagre and processed.
What I find structurally brilliant is that the passage never lets you be comfortable with your laughter.
These are desperate people — genuinely desperate, some of them — and Dickens knows it even as the jokes land.
The comedy and the tragedy are not alternating — they are the same thing at once.
That passage is a masterclass in comic taxonomy — the "inspired beggars," the "nobly independent beggars," the "beggars of punctual business-habits."
Each category is a perfectly observed human type, and each one is simultaneously pathetic and hilarious.
The man who will be "cold in death" at a quarter to one on Tuesday — with his "exact memorandum of the heartless circumstances" — I defy anyone not to laugh and wince simultaneously.
And the "beggars on horseback" — the ones who need only a clock or a violin or an astronomical telescope to gallop to fortune — these are recognisable human beings.
Dickens doesn't mock poverty; he mocks the particular forms that desperate ingenuity takes under pressure.
There's affection in it, even — a dark, uncomfortable affection.
I'd push back slightly on the affection — or at least qualify it.
Dickens's sympathy here is always conditional — conditioned on the poor behaving in ways that are legible and non-threatening to a middle-class reader.
But where this novel is genuinely radical — and I think more radical than Dickens himself understood — is in figures like Wegg.
Wegg finds the secret will, and what does he do with the power it gives him?
Dickens gives us the answer with remarkable clarity.

"Power, unless it be the power of intellect or virtue, has ever the greatest attraction for the lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg."
What Dickens is describing here is the psychology of the dispossessed given a fragment of leverage — and what it does to them.
The system has given Wegg nothing — and so the fantasy of destruction becomes his only form of power.
Dickens blames Wegg's nature, but the novel's evidence indicts the structure that produces such natures.
That tension — between Dickens's explicit moral verdict and what the novel actually shows — is precisely what makes him so interesting to read closely.
And the will itself — the document Wegg has found — is another of the novel's dark jokes about inheritance and worth.
Wegg reads it out to Mr Venus, and the terms are extraordinary in their contempt for human connection.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Quite enough for him" — the old miser's contempt for Boffin buried right there in the legal language.
This is a will that reads like a verdict — not on the heirs, but on the testator himself.
A man so isolated he has only the Crown to leave his fortune to — and even that he does in a tone of wounded grievance.
And Wegg reading that document aloud to Venus — that scene is almost vaudeville, but with something genuinely sinister underneath.
"Blandly and buoyantly" — that's how Dickens describes Wegg — and those two adverbs do more character work than a page of description would.
When I read Wegg, I always find that slightly bloated self-satisfaction — the man who has found his moment and intends to savour every syllable of it.
The dark comedy of this whole sequence is that every single person circling Boffin — the Duke, the inspired beggars, Wegg — believes they have found their legitimate claim on wealth.
And every single claim is fraudulent in its own particular way.
That's exactly right — and it's why the dust heaps function as such a perfect symbol throughout the novel.
Wealth itself in this novel is refuse — it accumulates through the sorting of what others have discarded, the labour of people who are never named.
And now that money has crystallised into Boffin's mansion, everyone from dukes to dying letter-writers wants to re-dissolve it into their own pockets.
The novel is relentless on this point: money in this world has no legitimate origin and no legitimate destination.
It simply moves — from the poor upward, always upward — dressed in the language of charity, or duty, or inheritance.
What strikes me listening to all three of you is how Dickens manages to make greed simultaneously hilarious and horrifying — and how that tonal balance never quite tips one way or the other.
The dust heaps made one man's fortune — and that fortune has turned the world around him into something resembling the dust heaps themselves: chaotic, stratified, and fought over by everyone.
Coming up, we'll look at how Dickens maps this world of greed onto the river — and onto the figures who make their living dredging it for the dead.

segments.title: Death and Resurrection: Harmon's Narrative Imposture

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're turning now to one of the novel's most elaborate structural games: the question of who John Harmon actually is, and what it costs him to be nobody.
Harmon returns from abroad, survives an attempt on his life, and chooses — for a remarkable stretch of the novel — to remain officially dead.
That choice puts him in the orbit of the Boffins, who are grieving the boy they once protected, and who have no idea the man standing before them is he.
Eleanor, Daniel, Oliver — I want to start with the emotional architecture of this section, because Dickens has done something quite unusual.
He gives us the Boffins' loyalty and grief before he gives us the revelation — and I think that sequencing matters enormously.
It matters enormously, and I think what Dickens is doing is front-loading the moral weight before the plot mechanics kick in.
We hear about the Boffins' loyalty through Boffin's own voice — this wonderfully guileless, unstoppable voice — and the details are almost grotesquely specific.
The black straw bonnet perched on Mrs Boffin's head as a matter of convenience — that single image does so much work.
Listen to how Boffin tells it to Lightwood — there's the setup, there's the spinning bonnet, and then that devastating short sentence at the end.
"Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — "Dropped her" — is Dickens trusting the rhythm to carry all the shock and sorrow that a page of description couldn't.
Two words, a full stop, then the same two words again — and the floor disappears beneath you.
I have to say, as someone who has read that passage aloud more than once, those two words are the hardest to get right.
If you rush them, you lose the weight entirely. If you overdo them, you turn tragedy into bathos.
Dickens has written it for a particular kind of silence after — and that silence is built into the punctuation.
But what strikes me even more is the comedy that surrounds it — the bonnet spinning across the yard, the sheer indignity of it.
Dickens is doing something very precise: making old Harmon monstrous and ridiculous simultaneously, so you feel the violence and the absurdity at once.
That's a very particular kind of genius — the grotesque as a delivery mechanism for moral seriousness.
I want to push slightly on the comedy, because I think there's a political logic underneath it that Dickens may not have fully intended.
Old Harmon is not just a cruel father — he is the novel's purest image of what hoarded capital does to a human being.
And Dickens gives us the key to understanding him in the Boffins' will passage — this extraordinary moment of clarity about how wealth actually works.
The narrator tells us that old Harmon had perceived — and this is the phrase that stops me every time —
"the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
There it is — the confession buried inside the will.
Money can buy almost everything in Dickens's London, but it cannot buy integrity — and old Harmon, for all his misanthropy, knows this.
That knowledge does not make him better. It makes him write a will — which is a very different thing.
That's exactly right, and it connects to something Mrs Boffin does in the very next chapter that I find almost unbearably moving.
She proposes adopting an orphan child and giving him the name of the boy she believes to be dead.
And she says it with such plain-spoken tenderness — this is her exact phrasing:
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She's doing something structurally remarkable here: trying to route the money back to the person it was meant for, even though she thinks he's gone.
And Dickens has placed this just before the revelation that John Harmon is alive — which means we read it with a dramatic irony she cannot feel.
The man she wants to memorialize through a name is standing somewhere in the same novel, breathing.
And that irony becomes structural punishment for Harmon in the later chapters, doesn't it.
Because when he does reveal himself — and the confrontation with Wegg is extraordinary — he has to account for everything that was done in his name while he was supposed to be dead.
The Wegg scene is magnificent. John Harmon finally gets to be himself — furious, physical, in charge — and there's a kind of release in it.
He tells Wegg precisely what was done to him and why — with a sailor-like grip on his cravat, mind you.
He says he kept Wegg "under good observation from my first appearance here" — and then the beautiful detail:
"Sloppy has long made it the chief occupation and delight of his life, to attend you like your shadow."
Sloppy — this great lumbering benevolent creature — shadowing the scheming Wegg through the dust heaps. It's a sublime comic image.
The Wegg confrontation is satisfying, but I think it's also where the novel's ideological seams show a little.
Wegg is a man of the margins — half a leg, a book-stall, a gift for versifying — and his crime is aspiring to property he has no claim to.
Harmon physically assaults him and declares — with what the narrator calls "the heartiest good will" —
"I'd give a thousand pounds for leave to knock your brains out."
One thousand pounds. The precise idiom of wealth deployed as the measure of righteous violence.
Dickens wants us to cheer this — and we do cheer it, because Wegg is genuinely odious.
But the restoration of legitimate property rights through physical force, narrated with approval — that's a conservative fantasy dressed in comic clothing.
Dickens the radical keeps bumping into Dickens the property owner.
I half agree with that — but I'd argue the deeper justice in this sequence isn't the violence, it's the information.
Harmon tells Wegg that the entire scheme was allowed to play out precisely to maximize his humiliation — to make the disappointment "the heaviest possible disappointment."
There's a kind of narrative sadism in that — and it mirrors Harmon's own position throughout the book, watching others grieve him, waiting for the right moment.
The impostor and the investigator share the same method: you let the deception run, you observe, you choose your moment.
Dickens is writing a moral thriller in the guise of a social novel — and Harmon's resurrection is the fulcrum of the whole machine.
That phrase — the fulcrum of the machine — feels exactly right for what Dickens is doing structurally here.
Harmon's secret organizes grief, loyalty, villainy, and eventual justice — all while the man himself stands silently at the center.
We've heard about the Boffins' extraordinary fidelity, Mrs Boffin's redemptive impulse, and Harmon finally speaking in his own person — with his hands around Wegg's collar.
In the next segment, we'll widen the lens and ask what the dust heaps themselves mean — as economy, as metaphor, as the novel's most original and unsettling image.

segments.title: Comic Grotesquerie: Laughter at the Margins

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we turn to one of the novel's most vertiginous qualities: the way comedy and darkness inhabit exactly the same space.
Dickens can move from the grotesquely funny to the genuinely harrowing within a single paragraph — and Our Mutual Friend may be the novel where he does this most recklessly and brilliantly.
Eleanor Hartley is with us — a novelist and craft critic who has been tracking the architecture of this book's narration with extraordinary precision.
Daniel Rosen reads every laugh in this novel as a transaction — he wants to know who is laughing, at whose expense, and what that tells us about the social machinery underneath.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has performed more Dickens than perhaps any living reader, hears the comedy in the prose rhythms themselves.
Eleanor, let's begin with you — because the passages you've been sitting with this week contain some of the strangest tonal mixtures in the whole novel.
Thank you — and yes, strange is exactly the word, because Dickens keeps wrong-footing you in these passages.
Take the passage where the narrator gives us Rokesmith's secret longing for Bella — this tender, almost unbearable interior wish.
But Dickens frames it with this ridiculous, endearing baby-talk address: 'O boofer lady, fascinating boofer lady!'
O boofer lady, fascinating boofer lady!
That's the language Bella's young admirer Johnny used before his death — Dickens imports a dead child's voice into an adult man's longing.
It's grotesque and it's heartbreaking and it's somehow funny, all at once — and that simultaneity is the Dickensian trick.

And then — and this is where the craft becomes almost audacious — he lets the narrator slide into a legal fantasy, as if Rokesmith's grief has to dress itself in the language of wills and receipts to be expressible at all.
Listen to how the passage reads:
If I were but legally executor of Johnny's will! If I had but the right to pay your legacy and to take your receipt!
Love rendered as probate law — it's comic and it's aching and it tells you everything about what money has done to feeling in this novel.
Eleanor, that phrase — 'to take your receipt' — when I first read it aloud I had to stop and laugh, because it's so preposterous and so exactly right.
It's the sound of a man so trapped inside the novel's own inheritance plot that even his private yearning has become a legal document.
But then Dickens does something I find almost mischievous — he lets the railway train share in the joke.
The stations are 'knowingly shutting up their green eyes and opening their red ones when they prepared to let the boofer lady pass.'
The whole Victorian railway network has become a conspirator in this man's secret love — winking at him as Bella goes by.
That's a comedian's instinct — you don't just tell the joke, you extend it until it has become a whole animated world.
I want to stay with that image of the railway for a moment, because I think it's doing something more unsettling than charm.
The railway is the great engine of Victorian capital — it moves goods, it moves people, it moves money.
And here it's conscripted into a private romantic fantasy built entirely around an inheritance.
The comedy doesn't dissolve the economics — it saturates them.
Rokesmith cannot imagine claiming Bella outside the terms of the will — not as a free man, but as executor, as payer of a legacy.
That is, I think, a tragic comic insight — love in this novel has been so thoroughly colonised by property that even its most private expression has to borrow the language of the counting house.
Daniel, that word 'colonised' — yes.
And I think you can see that same colonisation working in the Eugene Wrayburn passage I've been looking at — but in a very different register.
Eugene is explaining his pursuit of Lizzie Hexam to Mortimer, and the scene is ostensibly comic — Eugene performing his own laziness, his inability to think beyond the immediate moment.
But the comedy keeps curling back on itself to reveal something genuinely frightening.
He says — and this is one of those lines that reads as a bon mot until you think about it:
Fair means or foul means, are all alike to me. When I have found her I may ask you — also for information — what do I mean now?
He is confessing, in the most aesthetically pleasing way possible, that he has absolutely no moral constraints on his pursuit of this woman.
The wit is the disguise — and Dickens lets you see through the disguise and enjoy the wit simultaneously.

That phrase 'also for information' is one of the most perfectly placed comic beats in the whole novel — because of course he is asking Mortimer for information, as a man who genuinely does not know his own intentions.
The joke and the confession are completely fused — you cannot separate them.
When I read Eugene aloud, I always feel there's a kind of vertigo in him — he is performing detachment as a defence against having to feel anything.
And the reader laughs, and then stops laughing, and then is not entirely sure what they were laughing at.
That vertigo is, I think, class-specific — and I want to push on it.
Eugene's performed ignorance of his own intentions is a luxury available only to a man of his social position.
Lizzie Hexam cannot afford not to know her intentions — she is the object of his search, and his 'fair means or foul' will land on her body.
The comedy of Eugene's self-ignorance is, from Lizzie's perspective, something rather close to menace.
And Dickens, for all his apparent amusement, registers this — which is why the novel earns the darkness it eventually arrives at.
The darkness, yes — and the passages I've been given span the full range of it.
Because alongside the Rokesmith tenderness and the Eugene wit, there is Bradley Headstone — and Bradley is where the comedy has curdled entirely into something irreversible.
The narrator gives us a psychological anatomy of the murderer's mental state — not remorse, but something the novel names as worse than remorse.
The passage reads:
He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.
'Doing it more efficiently' — that phrase is devastating precisely because it contains no horror.
It's the language of a craftsman improving his work — applied to murder.
Dickens has made the comedy of competence grotesque — the very faculty that is comic in Eugene, systematic self-improvement, becomes a form of damnation in Bradley.
I find that passage almost unreadable aloud — in the best sense.
It has the syntax of analysis — measured, organised, step by step — but the content is a mind that has become its own torture chamber.
And what the narrator captures is this — without remorse, there is no release valve.
Guilt, at least, offers the possibility of confessing and being done with it.
Bradley gets the repetition without the catharsis — the act replayed and perfected forever in a mind that will not break.
There's a character who orbits Bradley in one of these passages who I think deserves more attention — Charley Hexam.
Charley confronts Bradley after the attack on Wrayburn, and what Dickens gives him is a speech of pure, unashamed self-interest — delivered with complete moral seriousness by Charley himself.
He says to Bradley — and the audacity of this is quite remarkable:
you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me.
Charley is accusing a would-be murderer of selfishness — for failing to consider Charley's social advancement while planning the crime.
It is one of the great comic monstrosities of the novel — but the comedy is indistinguishable from the social criticism.
Charley has internalised the logic of respectability so completely that he cannot see any event — including attempted murder — except through the lens of its effect on his prospects.
And the structural irony is perfect — because Charley has spent the novel lecturing Lizzie about her failure to pursue respectability, and now respectability's logic has produced this.

He has arrived at the endpoint of the ideology he has championed throughout — and the endpoint is a conversation with someone who has tried to kill a man, in which the chief complaint is insufficient consideration of Charley's career.
That's the grotesque functioning at full pressure — the laughter is completely and uncomfortably earned.
That image of laughter that is 'uncomfortably earned' feels like exactly the right place to pause on this thread.
In Our Mutual Friend, Dickens seems never to let comedy rest — it is always being converted into something else, or exposing something it didn't mean to.
In our next segment, we'll follow the novel's obsession with money and the Thames — the two great currents that everything else moves along.

segments.title: The Veil Between Worlds: Narrative Unreliability and Social Position

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — carefully, lovingly — and try to understand how it works.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel obsessed with disguise, with hidden identity, with the question of who is watching whom — and who has the power to tell the story.
Today we're looking at narrative unreliability and social position — the way Dickens uses secrecy, surveillance, and deception to expose how class shapes what we are permitted to know.
With me are three readers who bring genuinely different ways of seeing this material.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens the way a watchmaker reads a mechanism — for the precise beauty of the working parts.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who sees every act of concealment in a novel as a symptom of something the social order needs to hide.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic audiobooks than anyone has a right to be — brings the performer's instinct for what is written to be heard rather than merely read.
Let's begin with John Harmon — or Rokesmith, or whatever we should call him — and the extraordinary confession at the heart of these chapters.
What strikes me first about the Harmon confession is its narrative architecture — the way Dickens constructs a self-interrogating monologue inside the third-person novel.
Harmon is effectively putting himself in the dock and cross-examining his own testimony.

The details he assembles about Radfoot — Brussels, the French, the 'little history of himself' — are all offered under this hovering qualification: God only knows how much of it true, and how much of it false.
That uncertainty isn't incidental — it's structural.
The man who plots to observe others without being observed cannot himself be a reliable narrator of his own motives.
And then the plot itself — listen to how Dickens phrases it.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'

Those repeated gerunds — getting, throwing, trying — give the whole enterprise a helpless, unsteerable quality, as though the plot were something that happened to him rather than something he devised.
Eleanor's caught something I find absolutely irresistible on the page — the way Harmon ends that whole confession with what sounds like a courtroom stipulation.
He asks himself: 'I have all these facts right?' — and then answers: 'Yes. They are all accurately right.'
Two sentences. A question and an answer. Both from the same man.
As a performer, that's a gift — there's comedy in there, and terror, simultaneously.
A man so isolated by his disguise that he has become his own only credible witness.
I want to hold onto that phrase 'common sailors' dresses' for a moment, because it does a great deal of work.
Harmon can dress down precisely because he knows the disguise is temporary — the wealth waits for him like a coat he's left in the cloakroom.
What looks like a romantic adventure — spying on your intended bride — is actually an exercise of class power.
He gets to audit Bella without her knowledge. She has no equivalent right of inspection over him.
The information asymmetry is absolute — and it maps precisely onto the asymmetry of their economic positions.
That information asymmetry runs deeper in the next chapter, where Dickens gives us Rokesmith's full reckoning with what his deception has cost — and what it was originally meant to be.
Eleanor, that passage has a very particular emotional texture — almost like watching someone unpick a knot in slow motion.
That's exactly the sensation — Dickens writes it as an accumulation of conditionals and qualifications that mimics the experience of self-justification in real time.
The key sentence is this one — and it's very long, deliberately so.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
That clause — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is buried in the middle, and it is the whole case for Harmon in miniature.
His father's money had never produced a good outcome in his experience — not once.
So the distrust that drives the deception isn't vanity or cruelty — it's the logical residue of an entirely corrupted education.
And Dickens names the mechanism precisely — 'the misery-making money.'
'This is another of the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go.'
What's radical about that line is that the heir himself is diagnosing inheritance as an instrument of harm.
The wealth doesn't liberate — it corrupts everything it touches, including the intentions of the man who was meant to receive it.
And then the trap closes: he can't come to life without either buying Bella or punishing her.
The novel is almost clinical about it — wealth, once in motion, forecloses moral choice.
What I keep returning to is the phrase 'accumulated power of its separate circumstances' — Dickens is describing his own plot.
This is a novelist who understood that characters in novels, like people in life, rarely intend the full shape of the mess they eventually make.
And there is something quietly devastating about the moment he sees himself 'placarded by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead' — and simply accepts it.
Not with calculation — with the passivity of a man who has been trained by his whole life not to expect the story to go well for him.
There's a passage I'd like to bring in here that seems to crystallise all of this — the moment Rokesmith watches from a doorway as Betty Higden departs and Bella stands alone.
Oliver — as a performer, how do you hear that passage?
It's one of the most compressed sentences in the whole novel, and it's doing three things at once.
Let me read it, because it genuinely needs to be heard.

'The Secretary looked on from a doorway at the boofer lady thus encircled, and still looked on at the boofer lady standing alone there, when the determined old figure with its steady bright eyes was trudging through the streets, away from paralysis and pauperism.'
'Boofer lady' — Johnny's word for Bella, carried here from the child's death scene — it's an act of ventriloquism.
Dickens makes us see Bella through the eyes of a dead boy and a hidden man simultaneously.
And then that final phrase — 'away from paralysis and pauperism' — crashes Betty Higden's entire story into the end of the sentence like a stone.
The doorway is the structural image of the whole novel, isn't it — someone always watching from a threshold, never quite inside the scene they're observing.
Rokesmith's position here is precisely his position everywhere — he has access to intimacy but cannot participate in it without destroying his disguise.
And the repetition of 'looked on' — not watched, not observed, but looked on — has the quality of helplessness in it.
Betty Higden's presence in that sentence is not incidental.
She is trudging away from the workhouse — from state violence against the poor — while a rich man watches a beautiful young woman from a doorway.
Dickens places those two realities in the same sentence as a deliberate act of moral accounting.
The novel knows what it costs to look on — and who pays that cost.
From that doorway, let's move to another act of watching — and one of the most chilling sentences Dickens ever wrote about the corruption of a face.
Bella Wilfer looks at Mr Boffin — and what she sees is this.
'A dark cloud of suspicion, covetousness, and conceit, overshadowing the once open face.'
Daniel — that image of the corrupted face: what does it tell us about how Dickens understood the action of money on character?
The key word is 'overshadowing' — which implies that the open face is still there, underneath.
Boffin hasn't become evil — he's been obscured, covered over, by the atmosphere that wealth generates around a person.
That's an important distinction — Dickens is arguing that capitalism doesn't simply corrupt individuals, it produces a miasma that corrupts the way individuals appear to each other.
Trust itself becomes impossible in the world of money — you can never read the face, because money has intervened between the face and its observer.
And Dickens frames this through Bella's stealthy gaze — she 'ventured for a moment to look stealthily towards him under her eyelashes.'
This is the watcher who is also afraid of being watched — the observation is furtive, guarded, hedged.
The three-part catalogue — suspicion, covetousness, conceit — is classic Dickensian enumeration, but the rhythm here is more like a death sentence than a comic list.
Each quality is a stage in a progression — the suspicious man becomes covetous, the covetous man becomes conceited — and by the third term you feel the process is complete and irreversible.
What you lose in performance — what's very hard to convey — is how that sentence lands after chapters of Boffin's warmth and generosity.
The 'once open face' is doing enormous retrospective work — it makes you re-read everything you thought you knew about him.
And of course the novel will later complicate even this — Dickens is playing a very long game with the reader's capacity to trust what they observe.
The veil between worlds that Daniel is describing — the miasma of money — is also a veil between the reader and the truth of what is actually happening.
The veil, the doorway, the dark cloud — this is a novel that returns obsessively to the limits of what can be seen and known.
And we've only begun to trace it — we'll return after the break to look at what happens when those veils are finally lifted, and whether lifting them brings anything like freedom.
We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run beneath this great, strange, generous novel.
Before we close, I want to give each of our guests a moment to bring us back to the text itself — to the passages that, for them, carry the novel's deepest charge.
Eleanor, you've been sitting with a passage from early in the novel — Boffin remembering young John Harmon at seven years old.
This passage is, for me, one of the great hidden rooms of the novel — you almost stumble into it unprepared.
Boffin is telling the story in his own voice, his own syntax — that warm, slightly lumpen, utterly trustworthy voice.
And then Dickens gives him this image — the child's scanty travelling clothes, the scanty box, the shivering wind outside.
The repetition of that word — scanty — is doing something quietly devastating.
Boffin speaks, and listen to how the sentence opens:
That phrase — the wide wide world — is the language of a woman who cannot find a large enough word for what she feels.
And Dickens gives the whole scene to Boffin to narrate — this enormous feeling filtered through the simplest possible voice.
Eleanor has put her finger on something I feel every time I encounter that passage on the page — or on the microphone.
Boffin's speech rhythms are almost incantatory here — the parallel structures, the accumulation.
Listen to the end of it — what Dickens does with Mrs Boffin's sleepless nights.
That final phrase — it gently wore out, as many things do — that's an entire philosophy of grief in nine words.
Dickens is telling us that sorrow is not abolished — it is simply, slowly, absorbed into life.
What strikes me about that scene — and about the whole novel's ending — is the cost that the novel is willing to acknowledge even as it resolves.
The Boffins are kind people — genuinely kind — but they are, finally, the inheritors of a dust fortune, a fortune built on waste and labour.
And then there's this other passage I keep returning to — Lizzie speaking of a child entirely surrounded by ruin.
The line is almost clinical in its plainness — which is what makes it so severe.
That parenthesis — if she ever had one — is devastating in its brevity.
Dickens uses Lizzie's voice to say what the respectable narrative cannot quite bring itself to say directly.
There are children in this novel for whom no Boffin arrives, and the novel knows it.
And then Dickens turns the whole tension of class and appearance into pure comedy with Sloppy's suit.
Which sounds like a tonal lurch — but it isn't, because Dickens earns it.
The tailor is instructed to expend the utmost cunning of his art — to conceal the buttons.
And the result — listen to this:
The tailoring science defeated by the sheer frailty of Sloppy's form — that is Dickens at his most structurally cunning.
The body refuses to be dressed in respectability — it insists on itself.
That passage is an absolute gift to a reader aloud — you can feel Dickens timing the comedy.
Shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling — four verbs of light, each slightly absurder than the last.
And then the hatband — fluted behind, from crown to brim, terminating in a black bunch from which the imagination shrunk discomfited.
The reason revolted — as it well might.
But beneath the comedy — and this is what Daniel's been driving at all episode — Sloppy is a person whom the system has made conspicuous against his will.
His body won't submit. Even in his best suit, he cannot be hidden.
That's exactly it — and what the novel ultimately does with characters like Sloppy, like Lizzie, like the child without a cradle, is refuse to make them invisible.
Dickens cannot fix the system — he knows he cannot — but he insists on seeing everyone it has produced.
That's a political act, even when it arrives dressed in comedy.
Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, Oliver Trevelyan — thank you.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel that keeps refusing to be finished with you — and I hope this conversation has sent you back to its pages with fresh eyes.
From all of us at Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — thank you for listening.

‘My love,’ says Lady Tippins, ‘compose yourself; we’ll bring him in.’ And
      Lady Tippins really does work, and work the Veneering horses too; for she
      clatters about town all day, calling upon everybody she knows, and showing
      her entertaining powers and green fan to immense advantage, by rattling on
      with, My dear soul, what do you think? What do you suppose me to be?
      You’ll never guess. I’m pretending to be an electioneering agent. And for
      what place of all places? Pocket-Breaches. And why? Because the dearest
      friend I have in the world has bought it. And who is the dearest friend I
      have in the world? A man of the name of Veneering. Not omitting his wife,
      who is the other dearest friend I have in the world; and I positively
      declare I forgot their baby, who is the other. And we are carrying on this
      little farce to keep up appearances, and isn’t it refreshing! Then, my
      precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings
      are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the
      Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights. Curious to
      see ’em, my dear? Say you’ll know ’em. Come and dine with ’em. They shan’t
      bore you. Say who shall meet you. We’ll make up a party of our own, and
      I’ll engage that they shall not interfere with you for one single moment.
      You really ought to see their gold and silver camels. I call their
      dinner-table, the Caravan. Do come and dine with my Veneerings, my own
      Veneerings, my exclusive property, the dearest friends I have in the
      world! And above all, my dear, be sure you promise me your vote and
      interest and all sorts of plumpers for Pocket-Breaches; for we couldn’t
      think of spending sixpence on it, my love, and can only consent to be
      brought in by the spontaneous thingummies of the incorruptible
      whatdoyoucallums.
c20:p51.summary: Lady Tippins enthusiastically spreads the word about Veneering's candidacy, revealing her cynical view that the whole enterprise is a theatrical farce designed to keep up appearances, while openly admitting the Veneerings are unknowns with a spectacular house and ridiculous dinners.

‘It was only after a downward slide through something like a tube, and
      then a great noise and a sparkling and crackling as of fires, that the
      consciousness came upon me, “This is John Harmon drowning! John Harmon,

c51:p62.text:
The boat went on, under the arching trees, and over their tranquil shadows
      in the water. The bargeman skulking on the opposite bank of the stream,
      went on after it. Sparkles of light showed Riderhood when and where the
      rower dipped his blades, until, even as he stood idly watching, the sun
      went down and the landscape was dyed red. And then the red had the

‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.
c31:p109.best_quote: Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!

c38:p47.text:
‘Not a bit, my dear,’ said Mr Boffin. ‘But I think it’s very creditable in
      you, at your age, to be so well up with the pace of the world, and to know
      what to go in for. You are right. Go in for money, my love. Money’s the
      article. You’ll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin
      and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you’ll live and
      die rich. That’s the state to live and die in!’ said Mr Boffin, in an
      unctuous manner. ‘R—r—rich!’
c38:p47.summary: Mr Boffin emphatically advises Bella to pursue money above all else, declaring that she should capitalize on her beauty and the wealth they will bestow on her to become and remain rich.
c38:p47.best_quote: Go in for money, my love. Money's the article. You'll make money of your good looks, and of the money Mrs Boffin and me will have the pleasure of settling upon you, and you'll live and die rich.

c38:p55.text:
Somehow, Bella was not so well pleased with this assurance and this
      prospect as she might have been. Somehow, when she put her arms round Mrs
      Boffin’s neck and said Good Night, she derived a sense of unworthiness
      from the still anxious face of that good woman and her obvious wish to
      excuse her husband. ‘Why, what need to excuse him?’ thought Bella, sitting
      down in her own room. ‘What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very
      true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don’t I like it
      then? No, I don’t like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I
      disparage him for it. Then pray,’ said Bella, sternly putting the question
      to herself in the looking-glass as usual, ‘what do you mean by this, you
      inconsistent little Beast?’
c38:p55.summary: Alone in her room, Bella grapples with her confused reaction to Mr Boffin's advice: she finds his sentiments sensible and true to her own desires, yet she is repelled by them and finds herself disparaging him for expressing them, finally questioning herself severely in the mirror.
c38:p55.best_quote: Why, what need to excuse him? What he said was very sensible, I am sure, and very true, I am sure. It is only what I often say to myself. Don't I like it then? No, I don't like it, and, though he is my liberal benefactor, I disparage him for it. Then pray, what do you mean by this, you inconsistent little Beast?

The question was so directly at variance with Bella’s views in life, as
      set forth to her father, that she said internally, ‘There, you little
      mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain’t you ashamed of your self?’ and
      unclasped the girdle of her arms, expressly to give herself a penitential

c42:p156.summary: Bella experiences an internal moment of shame at her own mercenary values when confronted by Lizzie's selfless love, and literally punishes herself with a poke in the side.
c42:p156.best_quote: There, you little mercenary wretch! Do you hear that? Ain't you ashamed of your self?

c42:p162.text:
‘It was late upon a wretched night,’ said Lizzie, ‘when his eyes first
      looked at me in my old river-side home, very different from this. His eyes
      may never look at me again. I would rather that they never did; I hope
      that they never may. But I would not have the light of them taken out of
      my life, for anything my life can give me. I have told you everything now,
      my dear. If it comes a little strange to me to have parted with it, I am

c42:p162.summary: Lizzie recalls the rainy night she first met Eugene and confesses that sharing her feelings with Bella has been healing, though unexpected.

These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual

      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c40:p97.text:
For, Silas Wegg felt it to be quite out of the question that he could lay
      his head upon his pillow in peace, without first hovering over Mr Boffin’s
      house in the superior character of its Evil Genius. Power (unless it be
      the power of intellect or virtue) has ever the greatest attraction for the
      lowest natures; and the mere defiance of the unconscious house-front, with
      his power to strip the roof off the inhabiting family like the roof of a
      house of cards, was a treat which had a charm for Silas Wegg.
c40:p97.summary: Wegg cannot rest without hovering over Boffin's house, fantasizing about his power to destroy it, demonstrating how power appeals to base natures.
